working_title: How a Bakery Burned Down Most of London
hook: Ever accidentally burned toast so badly you nearly destroyed an entire capital city?

scenes.narration: Ever accidentally burned toast so badly you nearly destroyed an entire capital city?
It started past midnight on September second, 1666, in a tiny bakery on Pudding Lane.

scenes.narration: Step two: London was a giant wooden tinderbox with narrow streets and overhanging floors.
scenes.visual: flat 2D cartoon illustration, bold clean dark outlines, simple cel shading, bright warm colours, extremely narrow medieval London alleyway with timber houses leaning so close together their upper storeys almost touch across the street, a few confused citizens in funny hats looking up, simple readable shapes, detailed but uncluttered background, storybook comic look, no text

scenes.narration: Tara here! Houses practically hugged each other. Terrible for fire safety, great for gossip.
Step three: The Mayor panicked, hesitating to tear down houses due to rental paperwork.
scenes.visual: flat 2D cartoon illustration, bold clean dark outlines, simple cel shading, bright warm colours, a chubby mayor in a fancy fur-trimmed robe sweating profusely and holding his head in panic in front of burning timber houses, carrying a huge stack of paperwork, simple readable shapes, detailed but uncluttered background, storybook comic look, no text

scenes.narration: By the time he approved demolitions, a roaring wind turned the blaze into a firestorm.

scenes.narration: Step four: Panic! Rumours spread that foreign enemies tossed fireballs, causing total chaos.

scenes.narration: Old St Paul's Cathedral melted under the heat as the fire marched across the city.

Step five: London rose from ashes, keeping winding streets and teaching a fiery lesson.

structure: Countdown of the key moments that led to the outcome, building tension toward the final one.

claims.claim: Accidentally burned toast nearly destroyed an entire capital city
claims.note: The Great Fire started from a baker's oven left burning with brushwood by Thomas Farriner in Pudding Lane, not burned toast.

claims.claim: It started past midnight on September second, 1666, in a tiny bakery on Pudding Lane
London was a giant wooden tinderbox with narrow streets and overhanging floors
The Mayor panicked, hesitating to tear down houses due to rental paperwork
By the time he approved demolitions, a roaring wind turned the blaze into a firestorm
Rumours spread that foreign enemies tossed fireballs, causing total chaos
Old St Paul's Cathedral melted under the heat as the fire marched across the city
It stopped when wind died down and troops used smart gunpowder firebreaks
London rose from ashes, keeping winding streets

fact_check.summary: Most historical facts about the Great Fire of London are accurate, except for the popular myth that the fire started from burnt toast instead of a baker's oven.
